tasks.task_description: Develop a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, applied to the 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701, Alcaraz [player1] vs Djokovic [player2], 334 points, 5 sets). The model must (a) identify which player is performing better at a given time, (b) quantify how much better, and (c) provide the data for a visualization depicting the match flow. The serving advantage, which strongly raises the server's point-win probability, must be factored in. Scope: a per-point metric over the supplied dataset; the primary application is the featured final, with the metric also computed for the other matches in the test set.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) A player's 'form' at a point is its realized point-win rate over a recent window, and the fair benchmark for that rate is what a player of equal standing would be expected to win given who is serving and whether it is the first or second serve. (2) Points are conditionally independent given the serve state and the players' current standing (no hidden carryover is needed for the metric itself; carryover is tested separately in the next subtask). (3) The shot-detail columns (ace, winner, unforced error, net point, distance run, serve speed/width/depth, return depth) are partially coded: per expert exchange 1 a zero or blank in these columns means the detail was not logged for that point, not that the event was absent, so they are excluded from the flow metric entirely. Only the structurally complete core fields (point_victor, server, serve_no, scores, game/set victors, points won) drive the metric. Method. A logistic-regression baseline is fitted on all 31 matches (7284 points) to model the probability the server wins a point as a function of serve number (first vs second) and server identity. This yields a serve-adjusted fair baseline P(player1 wins point i) = p1_i for every point, which absorbs the large serving advantage. The flow of play is then the deviation of player1's recent realized point record from this fair baseline, expressed in units of its own null standard deviation, so it is a standardized 'how much better' measure that is comparable across points, matches, and set states. This is sound because the serving advantage is the dominant, well-known source of point heterogeneity in tennis; removing it leaves a residual that is approximately mean-zero under the null that both players hold constant form, which is exactly the property a flow-of-play indicator needs.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table (all empirical values are estimated from the supplied dataset; the two expert-supplied items are listed with their source exchange). (1) Baseline logit intercept b0 = 0.2162, interval estimated over all 7284 points / 31 matches, source: this dataset, logistic fit P(server wins | serve_no, server) = sigmoid(b0 + b1*serve_no + b2*server_id). (2) Second-serve effect b1 = -0.1802 (second serve lowers server's point-win probability), interval over the same 7284 points, source: this dataset. (3) Server-identity effect b2 = -0.0248, source: this dataset. (4) Implied P(server wins first serve) = 0.5539, P(server wins second serve) = 0.5090, source: this dataset. (5) Flow window W = 20 points, chosen on the 10-30 sweep where the metric is stable; the window is a modelling constant, interval [10,30] tested, source: sweep over the dataset. (6) Decision rule: a flow reading is treated as a candidate (not a confirmed) momentum signal, and is called actionable only when |flow| exceeds the 95th percentile of the block-permutation null AND it persists across the following several games; a one- or two-game edge is labelled noise, source: expert exchanges 2 and 3. Model. For point t let the most recent W completed points be indices t-W..t-1, with player1 win indicator x_i in {0,1} and baseline p1_i. Define the point excess S_t = sum_{i in window} (x_i - p1_i) and its null variance V_t = sum_{i in window} p1_i(1-p1_i). The flow metric is flow_t = S_t / sqrt(V_t), a z-score: positive flow means player1 is outperforming the serve-adjusted baseline (i.e. performing better), negative means player2 is, and the magnitude is the number of null standard deviations of the difference. p1_i is computed from the baseline logit using the actual server and serve_no at point i (if player1 serves, p1_i = sigmoid(b0 + b1*serve_no + b2); if player2 serves, p1_i = 1 - sigmoid(b0 + b1*serve_no - b2)). flow_t is NaN until W points have been played. The serving advantage is factored in through p1_i, so the metric measures form above and beyond the serve. Solution procedure: load and clean the CSV, fit the baseline on all matches, compute p1_i per point, compute flow_t per point with a rolling prefix-sum in O(n), and summarize per set and at set boundaries.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results for the featured final. The flow metric tracks the match narrative closely. Set 1: mean flow -1.26, flow at set end -1.31, Djokovic won the set 6-1 — player2 (Djokovic) clearly favored, matching the 'destined to win' description. Set 2: mean flow +0.07, flow at set end +0.15, a tense tiebreak set won by Alcaraz 7-6 — the metric stays near zero, correctly reflecting a genuinely even contest. Set 3: mean flow +0.75, flow at set end +1.99, Alcaraz won 6-1 — the strongest sustained flow in the match for player1. Set 4: mean flow +0.15 but flow at set end -1.27, Djokovic won 6-3 — the flow flips negative late in the set as Djokovic takes control, capturing the 'change of course'. Set 5: mean flow +0.06, flow at set end +0.08, Alcaraz won 6-4 — the flow hovers around zero, an even final set. The maximum |flow| in the match is 2.72 (at point 217, early set 4, when Djokovic's surge peaks). Overall point totals were nearly even (Alcaraz 168, Djokovic 166), so the match's swings came from timing and pressure, not total point volume — exactly what the flow metric reveals. Visualization: the flow_t series over the 334 points, with zero as the neutral line, positive region = Alcaraz favored, negative region = Djokovic favored, and the set boundaries marked, depicts the five swings (Djokovic lead, even, Alcaraz surge, Djokovic reclaim, even finish). Meaning and limitations. The metric identifies the favored player and its margin well and is interpretable as 'null standard deviations above fair.' Limitations: it is a lagging indicator (it reacts to the last W points, so it describes form that just happened rather than predicting the next point); it treats the baseline as fixed within the match, so a true skill drift over the whole match would be misattributed to short-term form; and because the window is 20 points, very rapid sub-game shifts are smoothed. Biases: the serving-advantage baseline is estimated on the same tournament, so it is well calibrated for these conditions but could be off for a different surface; and by construction the flow is a standardized residual, so its absolute scale depends on the window length and the baseline fit.

tasks.task_description: A coach claims that swings in play and runs of success by one player are random, i.e. that 'momentum' does not play a real role. Using the flow metric and the data, assess this claim: do the observed runs and swings exceed what a constant-skill (random) process would produce, or are they consistent with chance? Scope: the featured final primarily, with the test made robust to the window choice.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. The null hypothesis is the coach's: point outcomes are generated by a constant-skill, serve-adjusted process with no short-term momentum, so runs of the same victor and peaks in the flow metric are what random scatter produces. Per expert exchange 2, an elevated flow window is treated only as a candidate signal, not an established state; to distinguish real momentum from noise the test must compare the observed statistic to a null distribution that breaks short-range temporal structure while preserving the per-point marginal win rates. Method. Three complementary statistics are compared to their nulls. (1) Maximum |flow| over the match, the largest standardized deviation of player1's recent form. (2) The longest run of consecutive points won by the same player. (3) Forward persistence: among points where the current flow is strongly positive (>= 1.5 null-SDs), the fraction that are still strongly positive W points later; under the null the future flow is independent of the current one. The null is a circular block permutation of the point-outcome sequence within blocks of length W: this shuffles short-range order (destroying momentum-like runs) while preserving, within each block, the same multiset of outcomes, so the marginal win rate is held approximately fixed. 2000 block-permutation replications give the null distribution of each statistic; the observed value is significant at the 5% level only if it exceeds the 95th percentile of the null. This is sound because it directly tests the coach's claim (no carryover) against a null that has the same point totals and serve structure but no temporal dependence.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let won1_t in {0,1} be the indicator that player1 won point t, and let flow_t be the metric from subtask 1 with window W. Statistics. (a) M_flow = max_t |flow_t|. (b) L_run = the length of the longest consecutive block of identical values in the won1 sequence. (c) P_persist = (number of t with flow_t >= 1.5 and flow_{t+W} >= 1.5) / (number of t with flow_t >= 1.5). Null construction. For each of B = 2000 replications, split the won1 sequence into contiguous blocks of length W and randomly permute the outcomes within each block (circularly), producing won1*. Recompute M_flow*, L_run* and P_persist* from won1* using the same fixed baseline p1_i (the serve structure is unchanged because only the victor labels move within blocks). The p-value of an observed statistic is the fraction of replications whose null value is at least as extreme. Conclusion rule: the coach's randomness claim is supported if, at W = 20, all three observed statistics fall at or below their null 95th percentiles. Constants: W = 20 (model constant, tested over [10,30]); B = 2000 (Monte Carlo replications, a numerical choice); strong-flow trigger = 1.5 null-SDs (a threshold constant); decision threshold = 0.05 (the 95th percentile). All are recorded; none is taken from memory. Solution procedure: compute the three statistics on the observed final, run the block permutation to get the null distributions, and compare.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results for the featured final (W = 20). Maximum |flow| observed = 2.72 vs null 95th percentile = 3.16 (null mean 2.54) — the peak is inside the random range. Longest run observed = 7 points vs null 95th percentile = 11 (null mean 8.1) — well inside the random range. Forward persistence: of 22 points where the flow was strongly positive (>= 1.5 SD), 0% were still strongly positive 20 points later, versus a null mean of 6.3% and null 95th percentile 20.6% (p-value 1.0) — strong flow does NOT persist at all; it reverts. Conclusion: all three statistics are at or below their null 95th percentiles, so the observed swings and runs in this final are statistically consistent with the coach's random-process claim. The sweep confirms this is not a window artifact: at W = 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 the observed max |flow| (2.58, 2.34, 2.72, 2.30, 2.36) is below the null 95th percentile in every case and the longest run (always 7) is below the null 95th percentile (10-12) in every case, so 'random only' holds across the window range. Meaning: the dramatic swings the commentators attribute to momentum (Djokovic dominating set 1, Alcaraz surging set 3, Djokovic reclaiming set 4) are, at the point level, of the magnitude and frequency that a serve-adjusted random process would produce; the forward-persistence test additionally shows that a player 'in the zone' is no more likely to keep the zone than a coin flip. Limitations and caveats. The null preserves only first-order marginals and serve structure, so it cannot rule out momentum that operates through channels not in the data (fatigue, crowd, tactical adjustments, injuries) — the expert noted genuine short-lived form shifts do exist, and this test says the point-outcome signature of them is not detectable above noise in this sample. The forward-persistence statistic had only 22 triggers in one match, so its power is limited; the conclusion is that there is no evidence for persistence, not a proof of its absence. A single match is a small sample; the claim is assessed on the featured final and the finding is that its swings do not exceed random chance.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other. Using at least one match, build the predictor, identify which factors seem most related to swings, and advise a player going into a new match against a different opponent given the differential in past momentum swings. Test the model on one or more other matches and report how well it predicts the swings, what factors would improve it, and how generalizable it is to other matches, tournaments, surfaces, and sports such as table tennis. Scope: the model is developed on a pool of matches and validated out-of-sample on held-out matches (the featured final plus three others).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) A 'swing' in control of play is a game-to-game reversal: the game-level control value (the mean flow over a game's points, positive = player1 favored) changes sign and moves by at least 1.0 null-SD, so the favored player flips and the new favorite leads by at least one null standard deviation. This is a meaningful change of control, not a zero-crossing blip, and it is the object the coach wants to anticipate. (2) The state available at a game boundary (the flow value, its slope, the next server, break-point pressure in the game just played, the game length, the set and set-score context, and recent form) is what a player or coach can actually use to forecast the next game, so the predictor uses only boundary-available features. (3) There is no tautology: the feature set describes the state entering game t+1, while the label is the control of game t+1 itself, so the current flow does not appear inside its own prediction window. (4) Per expert exchange 3, a swing prediction is only actionable when it is corroborated by an observable trigger (e.g. break-point pressure) and is persistent; a lone statistical blip is treated as noise, so the model's output is framed as a candidate flag that must meet a corroboration gate. Method. A logistic-regression classifier is fitted on a pooled sample of 27 training matches (901 game-boundary observations) and evaluated on 4 held-out test matches (the featured final plus 1301, 1407, 1310) for a true out-of-sample assessment. Because swings are rare (base rate about 4-7%), the operating point is precision-oriented, and ranking quality (AUC) is reported alongside a threshold table so the result does not depend on an arbitrary cutoff. L2 regularization is used to keep the rare-event fit stable. This is sound because pooling across many matches gives the classifier enough swing examples to learn a signal if one exists, and holding out the featured match plus others gives an honest measure of how much of any learned signal transfers.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Game-level control. For each completed game g, control_g = (1/|g|) sum_{t in g} flow_t, the mean flow (in null-SDs) over the game's points. Swing label. For consecutive games, swing_{g+1} = 1 if sign(control_g) != sign(control_{g+1}) and |control_{g+1} - control_g| >= 1.0, else 0. Features at the boundary before game g+1 (all from core fields plus present/absent rally indicators, per the data-provenance handling): control (the control_g of the game just completed), slope (flow change across that game), next_server (who serves the upcoming game), game_bp (fraction of the just-played game's points that were break points), game_rally_hi (fraction of points with a long rally), game_diff (p1_games - p2_games), sets_p1, sets_p2, game_len (points in the just-played game), set (current set number). Model. swing = sigmoid(intercept + beta . features), fit by iterative reweighted least squares with L2 = 1.0. Solution procedure: build the control sequence and swing labels per match, pool the 27 training matches into one (X, y), fit the logit, then score the 4 held-out test matches and compute AUC, a threshold table, precision/recall, and the break-point corroboration rate of flagged swings. Constants: swing shift threshold 1.0 null-SD (a modelling constant, chosen so a swing is a real change of control); L2 = 1.0 (regularization, a numerical choice); decision/corroboration gate: flag only when the predicted probability is high AND break-point pressure (game_bp >= 0.25) is present, source: expert exchange 3. No empirical constant is taken from memory; all are either model constants or from the dataset/expert exchanges.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Out-of-sample results. Training AUC = 0.72 (901 game observations, base rate 4.4%); pooled test AUC across the 4 held-out matches = 0.58 (186 game observations, base rate 7.0%). The in-sample AUC is modest and, critically, it largely does not transfer: the test AUC of 0.58 is only barely above the 0.5 chance level. At every threshold in the table (0.2 to 0.7) the model flags at most one game in the entire pooled test set and that flag is a false positive, giving precision 0 at all operating points. Per test match: the featured final has 3 swings, 1301 has 2, 1407 has 2, 1310 has 6; the model flags none of them correctly. Verdict: the model is weak and, out of sample, essentially not predictive of game-to-game control swings. Factors most related to swings (by feature importance of the pooled fit): game_len (|beta|*std = 0.34), next_server (0.32), sets_p1 (0.22), control (0.14), and game_bp (0.13, with the largest single coefficient beta = 1.22). The break-point pressure feature carries the strongest individual coefficient, which is the one factor with a clear causal story (a break-point game is a natural pivot), but it is too sparse to drive the classifier on its own. Advice to a player going into a new match against a different opponent. Because the predictors do not transfer across matches (test AUC near chance) and because the past 'momentum' swings in this dataset are, per subtask 2, statistically indistinguishable from random, the evidence does not support carrying a specific momentum profile from one opponent or one match into the next. The defensible advice is therefore: do not expect to inherit or predict a particular swing pattern against a new opponent; instead prepare to recognize the few observable, in-match triggers that do recur (break-point situations and the server's change), respond to them with low-cost adjustments (reset routine, a tactical tweak) rather than dramatic mid-match changes, and treat any in-match 'flow' reading as a candidate signal that must be corroborated and persistent before acting — exactly the decision rule from expert exchange 3. How well it predicts and generalizability. The model predicts the swings poorly out of sample (test AUC 0.58, zero correct flags). Factors that would need to be included in future models: player- and shot-level information that is only partially recorded here (serve velocity and placement, winner/error type, distance run, net points), fatigue and time-of-day effects, crowd and surface context, and possibly a longer per-player history; the partially coded shot-detail fields limit the model. Generalizability: the negative result is itself the most transferable finding — if point-level swings are close to random in men's clay-free grass at this tournament, the same caution should apply to women's matches, other tournaments, and other surfaces, and by extension to other point-based sports such as table tennis, where the serving/point structure is similar and where one should likewise test for, rather than assume, persistent momentum. The baseline and swing definitions are surface-agnostic in form, so the same pipeline can be re-run on any point-by-point dataset; the specific coefficients will not.
